metadata.title: The value of a nomogram model combining ultrasonic features and blood inflammatory indicators in differentiating benign and malignant thyroid nodules

sections.text: This study aimed to investigate the value of clinical characteristics, conventional ultrasound features, and peripheral blood inflammatory markers in the preoperative differentiation of benign and malignant thyroid nodules and develop a nomogram-based predictive model. A total of 355 patients with thyroid nodules confirmed by surgical pathology or fine-needle aspiration cytology were retrospectively analyzed. Clinical data (gender and age), ultrasound characteristics, and peripheral blood inflammatory markers were collected. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were performed to identify independent predictors, which were used to construct a nomogram. The performance of the model was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic curves, calibration curves, and decision curve analysis. Multivariate logistic regression analysis showed that sex (male, odds ratio [OR] = 3.41), nodule shape (taller-than-wide, OR = 16.62), calcification (OR = 5.90), irregular margin (OR = 5.46), hypoechogenicity (OR = 4.75), hypervascularity on color doppler flow imaging (OR = 2.53), and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (OR = 4.23) were independent predictors of malignant thyroid nodules (all P < .05).The combined model (clinical data + ultrasound features + inflammatory marker) achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.850, which was higher than that of the clinical-data-only model (AUC = 0.546) and the clinical data plus ultrasound model (AUC = 0.831). The nomogram also demonstrated better agreement and greater net benefit in calibration and decision curve analysis. A nomogram integrating routine clinical information, conventional ultrasound characteristics, and neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio offers improved preoperative risk stratification for thyroid nodules. This tool demonstrates favorable discriminatory ability and potential clinical utility, and may complement existing ultrasound-based risk assessment systems.

Thyroid nodules are among the most commonly encountered endocrine system-related conditions in clinical practice. With the widespread adoption of high-resolution ultrasound technology and the continuous expansion of health screening coverage, their detection rate has been rising in recent years. [ 1 ] According to 2022 statistical data released by the International Agency for Research on Cancer, thyroid cancer has become one of the more common malignancies worldwide, ranking high in the number of new cases among the female population. [ 2 ] Although most nodules are benign, approximately 6.7–15% carry a risk of malignancy. [ 3 ] Accurately differentiating benign from malignant nodules in the preoperative phase is of significant clinical importance for optimizing indications for fine-needle aspiration, surgical decision-making, follow-up management strategies, and avoiding overtreatment. Currently, surgical pathology remains the definitive standard for diagnosing thyroid nodule malignancy. [ 4 ] Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC), as the most widely used preoperative minimally invasive assessment method, plays a key role in clinical risk stratification and treatment decision-making. [ 5 ] However, FNAC is inevitably affected by factors such as sampling location and operator experience, which may lead to false-negative or indeterminate results in some nodules. [ 6 ] Therefore, developing a noninvasive, quantifiable, and easily implementable auxiliary assessment tool based on routinely available preoperative information remains of practical value. Ultrasound examination is the primary imaging modality for evaluating thyroid nodules, providing direct visualization of morphological features and blood flow status. [ 7 ] Previous studies have confirmed that features such as hypoechogenicity, taller-than-wide shape (aspect ratio > 1), irregular margins, microcalcifications, and rich blood flow on color Doppler flow imaging (CDFI) are closely associated with an increased risk of malignancy. [ 8 , 9 ] Based on these typical sonographic findings, various ultrasound risk stratification systems have been proposed internationally, such as Chinese Thyroid Imaging Reporting and Data System (TI-RADS), American College of Radiology TI-RADS, and American Thyroid Association guidelines. [ 10 , 11 ] These systems are widely used in clinical practice and have demonstrated relatively stable overall diagnostic performance. However, differences in scoring rules and threshold settings among these systems still exist, and their interpretation can be somewhat operator-dependent. In cases with atypical ultrasound presentations or coexisting multiple nodules, relying solely on these ultrasound-based risk classifications (particularly for intermediate-risk nodules) may still have limitations. [ 12 ] In recent years, technologies such as radiomics and deep learning have advanced considerably. Artificial intelligence models based on ultrasound images have shown high diagnostic performance in some studies. Multiparametric approaches combining contrast-enhanced ultrasound or ultrasound elastography have also achieved promising results. In specific scenarios, the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve has exceeded 0.90. [ 13 , 14 ] However, these methods often rely on specialized software platforms, complex post-processing workflows, or the use of ultrasound contrast agents, demanding higher equipment conditions and technical support. Their applicability in primary care settings and routine health screening remains limited. [ 15 ] Meanwhile, studies have attempted to build combined prediction models by integrating clinical or laboratory indicators with conventional ultrasound classifications. Examples include combining TI-RADS with thyroid function parameters or blood inflammatory markers. These approaches have improved the ability to differentiate benign from malignant thyroid nodules to some extent. [ 16 , 17 ] Nonetheless, models in such studies often incorporate numerous variables and are relatively complex in structure. Moreover, the study populations have mostly focused on individuals already diagnosed or highly suspected of having papillary thyroid carcinoma, leaving the applicability and reproducibility of these models in broader nodule populations to be further validated. [ 9 ] Against this background, developing a preoperative risk assessment tool for thyroid nodules that is relatively simple in structure, noninvasive, and clinically operable (based on conventional ultrasound information combined with blood inflammatory markers) remains of significant practical importance. [ 18 ] Given this context, this study enrolled 355 patients with pathologically confirmed thyroid nodules. General clinical data, conventional ultrasound features, and peripheral blood inflammatory markers were systematically collected to explore their relationship with benign or malignant outcomes of thyroid nodules. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were performed to identify independent predictors. Subsequently, a nomogram prediction model integrating “clinical data(conventional ultrasound features) blood inflammatory markers” was constructed and validated. The aim is to provide a noninvasive, quantitative, operable, and widely applicable auxiliary assessment tool for preoperative risk stratification of thyroid nodules.

This was a single-center retrospective study, approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee. A total of 355 patients with thyroid nodules who underwent thyroid ultrasound examination at our hospital between January 2020 and June 2024 and had a definitive outcome determination were consecutively enrolled. Among them, 291 cases (82%) were confirmed by surgical pathology, and 64 cases (18%) were diagnosed based on FNAC results. In this study, surgical pathology served as the primary basis for outcome determination; for patients who did not undergo surgery, FNAC results were used. FNAC results were interpreted according to the Bethesda Reporting System, and only nodules with cytological diagnoses definitively classified as benign or malignant were included for outcome determination. [ 19 , 20 ] All cases had complete preoperative clinical data, ultrasound imaging records, and peripheral blood laboratory test results. Inclusion Criteria: underwent systematic thyroid ultrasound examination preoperatively, with image quality meeting analysis requirements; completed peripheral venous blood routine examination on the day of admission (within 24 hours); had a definitive diagnosis of benign thyroid lesion or differentiated thyroid carcinoma (including papillary carcinoma, follicular carcinoma, etc) confirmed by surgical pathology or FNAC; had complete clinical data, ultrasound imaging data, and blood routine examination results; to avoid statistical correlation bias caused by repeatedly including multiple nodules from the same patient, this study used the patient as the unit of analysis. Only 1 nodule per patient with a definitive outcome determination (surgical pathology or definitive FNAC diagnosis) was included for analysis. For patients with multiple nodules, all of which had definitive outcome determinations, a representative nodule was selected according to predefined rules: priority was given to the nodule with the highest number of malignant ultrasound features; if the number of malignant features was equal, the nodule with the largest maximum diameter was selected for inclusion. Exclusion Criteria: incomplete clinical data or suboptimal ultrasound image quality; recent infection, systemic inflammatory disease, or immune disease that might affect peripheral blood inflammatory markers; comorbid severe cardiac, hepatic, or renal insufficiency; received radiotherapy, chemotherapy, or glucocorticoid treatment preoperatively; history of or concurrent malignancy at other sites.

All patients were examined using a Philips EPIQ Elite color Doppler ultrasound diagnostic system with an eL18–4 transducer (frequency 4–18 MHz). The examinees were placed in a supine position with the neck fully exposed. The transducer was gently placed on the anterior neck region for multi-planar scanning of the thyroid gland. Instrument parameters were kept constant: focus depth approximately 3.0 cm, thermal index 0.2, mechanical index 0.9. Uniform parameters for CDFI were used: pulse repetition frequency 693 to 866 Hz, color gain adjusted to eliminate background noise, medium filter, and low-velocity flow mode. The following ultrasound features were recorded and analyzed: maximum diameter (cm); number of nodules (solitary/multiple); composition (solid/cystic); echogenicity (hypoechoic/iso- or hyperechoic); (5) shape (taller-than-wide, i.e., aspect ratio > 1/ ≤ 1); (6) Margin (regular/irregular); (7) Calcification (present/absent); (8) Echotexture homogeneity (homogeneous/heterogeneous); (9) Blood flow on CDFI (hypovascular/hypervascular). These ultrasound features were independently interpreted by 2 associate chief physicians, each with over 10 years of experience in thyroid ultrasound diagnosis, who were blinded to the pathological and cytological results. In case of disagreement, a third senior physician reviewed the images, and a consensus opinion was used as the final interpretation. General clinical data were collected via the hospital’s electronic medical record system. Preoperative blood routine test results, including neutrophil, lymphocyte, monocyte, and platelet counts, were extracted. Based on these data, blood inflammatory markers were calculated: neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio, lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio (LMR), and systemic immune-inflammation index (SII). [ 21 ] All laboratory tests were completed on the day of admission (within 24 hours) to ensure temporal consistency with the preoperative ultrasound assessment. [ 21 , 22 ]

All data analyses were performed using R software version 4.5.0 (R Foundation for Statistical Computing). Continuous variables were first tested for normality. Normally distributed continuous variables are expressed as mean ± standard deviation (𝑥 ± s), and compared between groups using the independent samples t-test. Non-normally distributed continuous variables are expressed as median M (Q1, Q3), and compared between groups using the Mann-Whitney U test. Categorical variables are presented as numbers and compared between groups using the χ 2 test or Fisher exact test. Using pathological outcome (benign = 0, malignant = 1) as the dependent variable, all continuous variables were entered into regression analyses in their original continuous form. General clinical data, ultrasound features, and blood inflammatory markers were separately included in univariate logistic regression analyses to screen for candidate variables associated with the outcome. Variable selection was based on a combination of statistical results, previous literature reports, and clinical relevance. [ 12 , 17 , 23 ] Variables that showed statistical significance ( P < .05) in univariate analysis and had clear clinical relevance were further entered into a multivariate logistic regression model. Stepwise regression was employed to identify independent predictors associated with malignant thyroid nodule outcome, and the corresponding odds ratios (OR) and their 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. Based on the independent predictors identified in the multivariate logistic regression analysis, a nomogram prediction model was constructed. The model underwent internal validation using the Bootstrap method (1000 resamples), and a calibration curve was plotted to assess the consistency between the model’s predicted probabilities and the actual outcomes. The discriminative ability of the model was evaluated via ROC curve analysis, and the area under the curve (AUC) was calculated. The DeLong test was used to compare differences in AUC between different models. To assess the clinical application value of the prediction model, Decision Curve Analysis (DCA) was further performed to calculate the net benefit across various threshold probabilities. All statistical tests were 2-sided, and a P value < .05 was considered statistically significant.

A total of 355 patients with thyroid nodules, all with definitive outcome determination, were included in this study. Among them, 291 cases (82%) were confirmed by surgical pathology, and 64 cases (18%) were diagnosed based on FNAC results. Overall, there were 225 benign nodules and 130 malignant nodules. In the malignant nodule group, there were 35 males and 95 females, with a mean age of (46.05 ± 12.19) years. In the benign nodule group, there were 40 males and 185 females, with a mean age of (45.42 ± 12.38) years. There was no statistically significant difference in age distribution between the 2 groups. All cases had complete imaging and clinical data. Malignant nodules were predominantly differentiated thyroid carcinomas, with the vast majority being papillary thyroid carcinoma and a small number being other subtypes of differentiated thyroid carcinoma.

The results of the univariate logistic regression analysis revealed that among the general characteristics, gender was associated with the risk of thyroid nodule malignancy. The risk of malignant nodules was higher in males than in females (OR = 1.70, 95% CI: 1.01–2.86). No significant association was observed between age and the risk of nodule malignancy. Regarding ultrasound features, univariate analysis showed that nodule shape (taller-than-wide, i.e., aspect ratio > 1), irregular margins, the presence of calcification, hypervascularity on CDFI, and hypoechogenicity were all significantly associated with malignant thyroid nodule outcomes. Their respective ORs (95% CIs) were 7.42 (4.35–12.66), 2.23 (1.42–3.52), 2.54 (1.62–3.98), 1.66 (1.05–2.61), and 2.00 (1.24–3.24). The association between the maximum nodule diameter and malignant risk did not reach statistical significance (OR = 0.69, 95% CI: 0.46–1.04, P = .08). Concerning blood inflammatory markers, the univariate analysis results indicated that lymphocyte count, NLR, LMR, and SII were associated with malignant thyroid nodule outcomes. Specifically, lymphocyte count and LMR showed a negative correlation with malignant outcomes, while NLR and SII showed a positive correlation. Associations between the remaining inflammatory markers (neutrophil count, monocyte count, platelet count, and platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio) and the outcome were not statistically significant ( P > .05) (Table 1 ).

Variables that were statistically significant in the univariate logistic regression analysis and had clear clinical relevance were included in the multivariate logistic regression model. The results of the multivariate analysis showed that gender, nodule shape (taller-than-wide, aspect ratio > 1), calcification, irregular margins, hypoechogenicity, hypervascularity on CDFI, and NLR remained independently associated with malignant thyroid nodule outcomes. Specifically, males had a higher risk of malignancy compared to females ( P < .001, OR = 3.41, 95% CI: 1.70–6.86). Among the ultrasound features, nodule shape (taller-than-wide) demonstrated the strongest association ( P < .001, OR = 16.62, 95% CI: 8.07–34.24). Additionally, calcification ( P < .001, OR = 5.90, 95% CI: 3.14–11.09), irregular margins ( P < .001, OR = 5.46, 95%CI: 2.87–10.39), hypoechogenicity ( P < .001, OR = 4.75, 95% CI: 2.44–9.25), and hypervascularity on CDFI ( P = .002, OR = 2.53, 95% CI: 1.40–4.58) were also significantly associated with malignant outcomes. Among the blood inflammatory markers, only NLR retained statistical significance in the multivariate model ( P < .001, OR = 4.23, 95% CI: 2.24–7.97), while LMR and SII did not show independent correlations after adjusting for other variables. Based on the independent predictors identified in the multivariate logistic regression analysis, a nomogram model for predicting benign or malignant thyroid nodules was constructed according to the relative magnitude of the regression coefficients for each variable (Fig. 1 ). The nomogram integrates gender, 5 key ultrasound features (nodule shape, calcification, margins, echogenicity, and CDFI vascularity), and NLR to provide a quantitative prediction of malignant risk for individual thyroid nodules.

To evaluate the impact of different variable combinations on the ability to differentiate between benign and malignant thyroid nodules, 3 prediction models were constructed: Model 1 (gender only), Model 2 (gender + ultrasound features), and Model 3 (gender + ultrasound features + NLR). ROC curves were plotted for comparison. The ROC analysis results showed: Model 1 AUC = 0.546, Model 2 AUC = 0.831, Model 3 AUC = 0.850 (Fig. 2 ). This indicates that the discriminative ability of the model was further enhanced after incorporating NLR into the traditional ultrasound-based model.

Internal validation of each prediction model was performed using the Bootstrap method (with 1000 resamples), and calibration curves were plotted to assess the agreement between the model’s predicted probabilities and the actual outcomes. The results showed that the calibration performance of Model 1 was relatively poor. The calibration of Model 2 showed significant improvement. The calibration curve of Model 3 was closest to the ideal reference line, indicating good consistency between its predicted probabilities and the actual outcomes (Fig. 3 ).

DCA was further employed to evaluate the clinical application value of the different prediction models across various threshold probabilities. The results showed that within a certain range of threshold probabilities, the net benefits of both Model 2 and Model 3 were higher than the reference strategies of “treat-all” and “treat-none.” Among them, the net benefit curve of Model 3 was overall higher than that of Model 2, while the net benefit of Model 1 gradually decreased as the threshold probability increased (Fig. 4 ). These results indicate that the prediction model combining ultrasound features and NLR holds superior potential application value in clinical decision-making.

Based on 1000 iterations of stratified Bootstrap resampling, the AUC values of the 3 predictive models were assessed for robustness, and their differences were compared. The results showed that, compared to Model 1, the AUCs of Model 2 and Model 3 increased by 0.292 (95% CI: 0.231–0.350) and 0.312 (95% CI: 0.252–0.368), respectively. Compared to Model 2, the AUC of Model 3 further increased by 0.021 (95% CI: 0.004–0.045) (Table 2 ). The results of the DeLong test indicated that, even after Bonferroni correction, the differences in AUC between the models remained statistically significant (all P < .05).

sections.section: 3.5. Clinical Application Examples Of The Prediction Model
sections.text: Two patients with thyroid nodules were selected to demonstrate the application of the nomogram prediction model in a clinical setting. Case 1 was a 40-year-old female. The nodule exhibited an aspect ratio ≤ 1, absence of calcification, regular margins, isoechogenicity, and no significant blood flow on CDFI (Fig. 5 ). The NLR was 2.0. Based on the nomogram, the total score was 20 points, corresponding to a predicted probability of malignancy < 0.1. Postoperative pathology confirmed a hyperplastic thyroid nodule. Case 2 was a 55-year-old male. The nodule demonstrated an aspect ratio > 1, presence of calcification, irregular margins, hypoechogenicity, and significant blood flow on CDFI (Fig. 5 ). The NLR was 2.8. According to the nomogram, the total score was 246 points, corresponding to a predicted probability of malignancy > 0.9. Postoperative pathology confirmed papillary thyroid carcinoma.

Thyroid nodules are frequently detected in clinical practice, and their preoperative differentiation between benign and malignant directly influences the formulation of indications for fine-needle aspiration, surgical decision-making, and follow-up strategies. [ 10 ] However, for nodules with atypical imaging presentations or those classified as intermediate risk, reliance solely on ultrasound-based risk stratification systems for preoperative decision-making still carries a degree of uncertainty. [ 9 , 12 ] Against this background, this single-center retrospective cohort study integrated patient clinical data (gender), conventional ultrasound imaging features, and NLR to construct and validate a nomogram prediction model for preoperative risk assessment of thyroid nodules. The results showed that incorporating NLR into a baseline prediction model consisting of clinical data (gender) and traditional ultrasound features led to a small but statistically significant improvement in model discrimination. This combined model also demonstrated additional net benefit in DCA, suggesting its supplementary value to existing ultrasound evaluation systems. In the multivariate logistic regression model established in this study, conventional ultrasound imaging features remained the core foundation for preoperative risk assessment of thyroid nodules. The results indicate that nodule shape (taller-than-wide, aspect ratio > 1), calcification, irregular margins, and hypoechogenicity maintained stable independent associations with malignant outcomes even after accounting for patient gender and blood inflammatory markers. Among these, nodule shape exhibited the strongest association (OR = 16.62), suggesting its relatively central discriminatory value in a multi-feature combined assessment. The OR values for ultrasound features such as calcification, irregular margins, and hypoechogenicity were also at relatively high levels (OR range approximately 4.75–5.90), further supporting the stability of their association strength in malignant thyroid nodules. These findings are generally consistent with conclusions from systematic reviews and network meta-analyses of grading systems like American College of Radiology TI-RADS and EU-TI-RADS. [ 10 , 11 ] Regarding vascular parameters, hypervascularity on CDFI retained independent correlation in the multivariate model, indicating it can provide supplementary information for preoperative risk judgment beyond grayscale ultrasound features. Among the blood inflammatory markers, only NLR maintained an independent association with malignant thyroid nodule outcomes in the multivariate logistic regression model, while markers like LMR and SII lost their independent predictive properties after incorporating gender and ultrasound features. [ 17 ] This finding aligns substantially with previous research, [ 23 ] suggesting that among coexisting blood inflammatory indicators, the inflammatory-immune state reflected by NLR may possess more stable independent predictive performance. From a model performance perspective, the inclusion of NLR led to a small but statistically significant improvement in the discrimination of the prediction model compared to the baseline model (ΔAUC = 0.021, 95% CI: 0.004–0.045). It is important to note that in models where the baseline AUC is already high, the incremental AUC gain from a new variable is typically limited. Nevertheless, previous methodological studies have indicated that even a small but stable improvement in AUC within a high-baseline performance model can still translate into practical benefits in specific decision-making contexts. [ 14 , 24 ] The DCA results in this study showed that within a certain range of threshold probabilities, the model incorporating NLR achieved a modestly higher net benefit compared to the model without blood inflammatory markers. This finding suggests that the addition of NLR may offer complementary information to support clinical decision-making in select scenarios, particularly for thyroid nodules with uncertain benign or malignant status. From a clinical application perspective, NLR is derived from routine blood tests, adding no extra examination burden. [ 25 ] Its introduction does not significantly increase model complexity, making it more suitable as a supplementary risk indicator on top of routine ultrasound evaluation. In recent years, several studies have attempted to combine ultrasound imaging features with clinical or laboratory indicators to construct nomogram models for thyroid tumor risk assessment. [ 14 , 24 ] For instance, Tang et al built a prediction model based on ultrasound features combined with thyroid function indicators and inflammatory parameters, focusing primarily on populations already diagnosed or highly suspected of having papillary thyroid carcinoma. [ 16 ] Qiao et al combined multiple inflammatory indicators in thyroid cancer patients to construct models for predicting tumor invasiveness or lymph node metastasis risk. [ 24 ] While these studies achieved good predictive performance within their specific study populations, their scenarios were often more oriented towards post-diagnosis or high-suspicion stages. In contrast, this study enrolled a “general thyroid nodule” population with definitive pathological or FNAC outcome determination, including both benign nodules and differentiated thyroid carcinomas. This research scenario more closely aligns with the real-world clinical dilemma faced at decision points such as whether to perform aspiration or further intervention for initially diagnosed nodules. It should be noted that some previous studies, by introducing contrast-enhanced ultrasound, radiomics, or artificial intelligence methods, obtained high model discrimination performance in specific study populations. [ 26 ] However, these often rely on contrast agent use or specialized technical platforms, making them more suitable for further examination or refined stratification stages. [ 13 , 15 ] In comparison, this study focuses on the routine assessment scenario for initially diagnosed nodules, emphasizing the integration and expression of risk information without increasing examination complexity. In summary, based on a single-center retrospective cohort, this study integrated patient clinical data (gender), conventional ultrasound imaging features, and the NLR to construct and validate a nomogram prediction model for the preoperative risk assessment of thyroid nodules. The results indicate that this model can provide incremental value both statistically and in terms of clinical decision-making. It holds promise as a supplementary tool to existing ultrasound-based risk stratification systems, offering a more intuitive and quantifiable reference for the preoperative risk stratification of newly diagnosed thyroid nodules.

This study also has certain limitations. First, as a single-center retrospective study, it may be susceptible to selection bias and information bias. The generalizability of the findings requires further validation through multi-center, large-sample prospective studies. Second, the outcome determination in this study was primarily based on surgical pathology results, with approximately 82% of cases confirmed by surgical pathology and the remaining 18% determined based on FNAC results. Although FNAC is widely used for preoperative risk stratification of thyroid nodules, and this study strictly limited inclusion to nodules definitively diagnosed as benign or malignant according to the Bethesda System, the risk of outcome misclassification due to false negatives or sampling errors cannot be entirely excluded. This type of potential misclassification is more likely to lead to a conservative estimation of the model’s predictive performance rather than an overestimation of its efficacy. [ 20 ] Furthermore, this study only conducted internal validation, and the interpretation of ultrasound features may still be influenced by operator experience and equipment differences. The external applicability of the model needs further verification in multi-center cohorts.

In conclusion, this study developed and internally validated a nomogram model that integrates easily accessible preoperative parameters: patient gender, conventional ultrasound features, and the NLR: for the individualized risk assessment of thyroid nodules. The model demonstrates good discriminatory ability, calibration, and potential net clinical benefit. It offers a practical, noninvasive, and quantitative tool that may serve as a valuable adjunct to existing ultrasound-based risk stratification systems, potentially aiding clinicians in the preoperative decision-making process for patients with thyroid nodules, particularly in cases of indeterminate or intermediate risk. Future multi-center prospective studies are warranted to further validate and refine its generalizability and clinical utility.
